π0.7 · April 2026

π0.7 and the Difference a Robot Coach Makes

Physical Intelligence’s π0.7 uses richer prompts to combine diverse robot experience. Its appliance experiments suggest a practical route to new skills, but coaching and unaided generalization need separate scorecards.

THE SHORT VERSION

  • Coaching can be a useful capability without being mistaken for unaided autonomy.
01 / CLOSER READING

Watch the help, not only the hands

A robot loading a sweet potato into an air fryer is a compact test of a very large claim. The scene requires recognizing an appliance, choosing a sequence, manipulating unfamiliar parts, and knowing when a step has worked. Physical Intelligence’s April 2026 π0.7 report provides an especially useful comparison: a single instruction yields a partial attempt, while step-by-step language coaching makes execution more effective.

That difference is not a reason to dismiss the result. It identifies the interface through which a person can contribute missing task knowledge. But it also means that “the robot completed the task” is an incomplete description. Before judging generalization, we need to know who supplied the plan, when they supplied it, and whether the system was adapted afterward.

In this section: [1]

02 / CLOSER READING

Prompting describes a strategy, not just a destination

The technical paper unifies several forms of context for a vision-language-action model: task language, more detailed instructions, visual subgoals, control-mode labels, and episode metadata. The metadata can describe qualities such as speed and performance. This lets training distinguish behaviors that should not be treated as equally desirable, including suboptimal autonomous experience.

At execution time, a human coach or a high-level policy can provide the next subtask; a world model can supply a visual subgoal. The action model combines context with observations to produce motion. Our interpretation is that prompting becomes a routing interface through the model’s experience. “What should happen?” and “How should it happen?” become different pieces of information rather than one overloaded sentence.

In this section: [2]

03 / CLOSER READING

There are three different achievements here

The release demonstrates unfamiliar appliance tasks with coaching, and describes fine-tuning a high-level policy from that coaching for later autonomous execution. It also reports laundry folding on a two-arm UR5e system without collecting laundry-folding examples on that particular robot. These are meaningful but different forms of transfer.

The authors additionally found related air-fryer interactions in the broader training collection. That is important context: a new combination of familiar ingredients is not the same as a completely unseen object or action. We would therefore describe the evidence in separate columns—single-instruction execution, coached execution, and execution after adaptation—rather than compressing all three into one success claim.

In this section: [1]

04 / CLOSER READING

Why a high-level policy changes the accounting

This division of labor has a clear predecessor in Physical Intelligence’s Hi Robot work. A high-level vision-language model interprets instructions and feedback, then issues simpler commands to a lower-level action policy. The design gives task decomposition an explicit place in the system instead of expecting one reactive policy to solve every semantic problem at once.

For evaluation, that means the planning layer is not invisible scaffolding. If it was trained for the appliance, its contribution belongs in the description. If a human generated the steps, that labor belongs in the measurement. Neither condition makes the lower-level capability uninteresting. It changes which capability has been demonstrated and which deployment burden remains.

In this section: [3]

05 / CLOSER READING

The missing scorecard is the cost of assistance

Our proposed test would hold out appliances, rooms, and coaches. The coach should receive a fixed instruction budget and should not quietly restart failures until a clean video appears. Record interventions, pauses, recoveries, and completed task stages. A system that succeeds with a small clarification is different from one that requires a person to supervise every grasp.

We would also include deliberately ambiguous instructions. Does the robot ask for clarification, choose a reasonable interpretation, or continue confidently with the wrong object? That matters because useful language following includes managing uncertainty, not merely complying with detailed commands. These are questions for a next experiment, not failures established by the existing demonstrations.

Finally, transfer the coached procedure to a second environment without silently adding new training. A useful result would reveal what the model retained: a transferable procedure, a dependence on visual layout, or a sequence that works only when the same person guides it.

06 / CLOSER READING

A practical interface, with an honest boundary

For builders, the attractive possibility is that explaining a task could sometimes replace collecting another full set of teleoperated demonstrations. Our judgment is conditional: the interface becomes valuable when the reduction in demonstration work exceeds the new costs of coaching, verification, and exception handling. That comparison should be measured rather than inferred from a successful clip.

The broader takeaway is to treat assistance as a design variable, not an embarrassment to remove from the headline. A capable robot and an effective coach can form a useful system before the robot is fully independent. The research becomes easier to understand when we say precisely which parts of that partnership have generalized, and which still depend on task-specific help.

TAKE IT TO THE ROOM

When does human coaching count as generalization, and when should we call it task-specific training?
